title: Constant-factor treewidth preservation by subcubic subgraphs
formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C\ge 1\) such that every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G contains a nonempty subgraph H with maximum degree at most 3 and \(\operatorname{tw}(H)\ge \operatorname{tw}(G)/C\)?
definitions: A subgraph \(H=(V_{H},E_{H})\) satisfies \(V_{H}\subseteq V(G)\) and \(E_{H}\subseteq E(G)\cap \{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V_{H},u\ne v\}\). Edges and vertices may be deleted, but no edge is contracted and no new vertex or edge is introduced. H need not be induced, connected or spanning. Its maximum degree is \(\max _{v\in V_{H}}|\{u:\{u,v\}\in E_{H}\}|\). A tree decomposition of a nonempty graph F consists of a finite tree T with vertex bags \(B_{t}\subseteq V(F)\), such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of each edge lie in a common bag, and the nodes whose bags contain a fixed vertex induce a nonempty connected subtree. Its width is \(\max _{t}|B_{t}|- 1\). Treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(F)\) is the minimum width over all such decompositions; nonempty edgeless graphs have treewidth zero. C is independent of G and its treewidth. No bound on the number of vertices of H and no construction-time requirement is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
why: Determine whether large treewidth always has a bounded-degree witness with only constant loss.

importance.reason: A structural sparsification principle for a central graph parameter; the gap concerns universal preservation rather than a particular construction.

progress.text: Chekuri and Chuzhoy establish degree-three subgraphs retaining treewidth up to a polylogarithmic factor.
Bonnet’s work on induced sparse subgraphs still cites polylogarithmic-loss treewidth sparsifiers as the available general degree-three guarantee.

context_blocks.text: Treewidth measures how far a graph is from having a tree-like organization. This question asks whether its full scale can always be retained after reducing every vertex degree to at most three.

The known degree-three sparsifier guarantee loses a polylogarithmic factor in treewidth. A universal constant would give a stronger structural witness regardless of the original graph’s density or degree distribution.

The target does not ask for an induced subgraph, a small number of vertices, or a grid minor. These additional output restrictions define different problems; arbitrary subcubic graphs need not have grid structure.

sentences: Every graph is asked to contain a subgraph of maximum degree three with comparable treewidth.
Comparable means losing only a universal constant factor.
The subgraph can delete edges and vertices but cannot contract edges or introduce new ones.
Known general degree-three sparsifiers lose a polylogarithmic factor in treewidth.
A constant-factor theorem would make bounded-degree structure a universal witness of large treewidth.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The 2025 paper and current question list retain the gap between polylogarithmic and constant loss; no general constant-factor theorem was found.
